approachQuestion.prompt:
Selecting nonconflicting broadcasts

An editor may keep some of n proposed half-open broadcasts [start,end). Every retained broadcast has equal value. Return the maximum number that can be kept on one channel with no overlaps. Touching endpoints are compatible. Proposals are unsorted; do not modify the input. Return only the count.

Input: broadcasts = [[0,7],[1,3],[3,5],[5,8]]
Output: 3
Keep [1,3), [3,5), [5,8).

Input: broadcasts = [[2,6],[2,6]]
Output: 1

Constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; integer endpoints satisfy 0 ≤ start < end ≤ 1000000000. Use comparison-based ordering. Choose the best worst-case running time; among equal-time methods prefer less auxiliary storage.

options.text: Sort copied broadcasts by end. Keep a broadcast whenever its start is at least the last kept end, beginning with no previous end. Return the number kept.
options.feedback: An earliest-finishing compatible choice leaves at least as much room for every later choice as another first choice. Repeating that exchange argument maximizes the number of broadcasts.

options.text: Sort by start and keep each compatible broadcast.
options.feedback: For [[0,7],[1,3],[3,5],[5,8]], keeping [0,7) prevents all three shorter broadcasts, producing 1 instead of 3.

options.text: Process broadcasts from shortest duration to longest, keeping each if it conflicts with none already kept.
options.feedback: For [[0,3],[3,6],[2,4]], the shortest [2,4) blocks both others. It keeps 1 when [0,3) and [3,6) allow 2.

options.text: Try every subset, test pairwise compatibility, and return the largest compatible size.
options.feedback: This returns the correct optimum, but enumerates an enormous number of subsets. Equal values and interval structure allow a direct safe selection rule.

feedback.reason: Use an exchange argument for earliest finishing rather than earliest starting or shortest duration.
details: Create a copy, sort it by end with iterative bottom-up merge sort and one reusable buffer, then scan it once holding only the last accepted end and a count.

Earliest finish is safe by exchange: replacing a chosen first broadcast with an earlier-finishing one leaves every later compatible broadcast available. Earliest start and shortest duration do not provide that guarantee.

“Sort copied broadcasts by end. Keep a broadcast whenever its start is at least the last kept end, beginning with no previous end. Return the number kept.”: An earliest-finishing compatible choice leaves at least as much room for every later choice as another first choice. Repeating that exchange argument maximizes the number of broadcasts.
“Sort by start and keep each compatible broadcast.”: For [[0,7],[1,3],[3,5],[5,8]], keeping [0,7) prevents all three shorter broadcasts, producing 1 instead of 3.

“Process broadcasts from shortest duration to longest, keeping each if it conflicts with none already kept.”: For [[0,3],[3,6],[2,4]], the shortest [2,4) blocks both others. It keeps 1 when [0,3) and [3,6) allow 2.

“Try every subset, test pairwise compatibility, and return the largest compatible size.”: This returns the correct optimum, but enumerates an enormous number of subsets. Equal values and interval structure allow a direct safe selection rule.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For earliest-finish-selection, n is the proposal count. Count the input copy and sort buffer, but not the returned integer. Choose the tightest standard worst-case pair.
constraints: Analyze only the named method. Count all temporary arrays and the call stack; exclude the supplied input and returned output. Numeric comparisons, assignments and arithmetic take constant time, with no overflow.
No hashing or amortized data structure is used. All loops and binary searches are iterative; there is no recursive stack.

options.text: Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n)
Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(log n)

feedback.reason: Sort by finish and make one linear compatibility scan.
details: The one-pass selection is linear. Comparison merge sort of the copy requires O(n log n) time and a reusable O(n) buffer; the copy is also O(n). There is no recursive stack. Exhaustive subset search is unnecessary.
Immutable input; copied records; iterative bottom-up merge sort.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(1)”: The unsorted input must first be copied and comparison-sorted; a constant-state scan describes only the final phase.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(1)”: The algorithm does not test all pairs. Sorting followed by a forward pass gives a tighter time bound.
“Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(log n)”: Even without recursion, the copied records and iterative merge buffer occupy linear space, exceeding a logarithmic bound.
